evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney.** Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone. Observations: U20, U48.
- **Provisional applications doubled in FY2026.** 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, mostly from individuals but from organisations too, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is in the filings, not the recording. Why is a question for IP Australia. Observations: U8.
- **Around some policy changes, filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses.** Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.41 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began; around other changes nothing stands out. These timings are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need. Observations: U28, U3.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Filing without an attorney still goes with far fewer grants.** With the route, year, state and co-filers held together, Australian individuals' patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often (35.8 raw), in both decades; trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it. Not a cause: an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: M1, M2.
- **Australian organisations' patents: three readings that still disagree.** At the same reach they are less likely to end (hazard ratios 0.648 to 0.811), yet they reach fewer offices and are cited about 27% to 30% less at the same reach, field, route and year. None of the three is value; they must be read together. Observations: M3, M4.

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Filing without an attorney goes with poorer outcomes.** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 percentage points less often, in both decades and among examined applications too. Australians' trade marks with no agent before the first renewal stay in force less often (19.1 points). The arrow may run backwards: an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: B5, B6, B10.
- **Some inventions made here are filed or held overseas.** About one patent in seven with an inventor in Australia is filed from overseas. Australian-filed patents now held only overseas are more common among the wide and the granted, though by firm the youngest filers are not clearly different. Few of the US patents citing Australian research have an Australian party, but a citation is not use, so none of this shows where value is realised. Observations: B16, B19, B26, B46.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **id**: M1
- **title**: An example: filing without an attorney
- **intro**: Stage 2 found Australian individuals' patents filed alone granted about 36 points less often (B6). Stage 3 held the route, filing year, state and co-filers together.
- **text**: Grey dots are the raw gaps, blue the gaps with those factors held, each with its interval. For individuals 87.2% of the gap is left in FY2010 to FY2019, and 86.2% in the decade before: it holds. For Australian organisations in FY2000 to FY2009 both intervals cross the line of no difference: not detected either way.

evidence.title: M1: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often once the factors settled at filing are held together
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Take Stage 2's comparison (filed alone against with an attorney) as the raw figure.
2. Fit one model of the yes or no outcome (granted or not) with the route, filing year, state and co-filers held together, and report the difference as an average difference in points.
3. Compare the held figure with the raw one, and give the outcome by Stage 3's rule (holds if at least half remains and the interval is clear of zero).
4. Repeat in the earlier decade, among applications with a field (holding the field), and among examined applications.

**Which gives observation M1:** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often than those filed with an attorney once the route, filing year, state and co-filers are held together (FY2010 to FY2019), against 35.8 points with nothing held: 87.2% of Stage 2's gap remains, and 86.2% in the earlier decade. Trade marks filed alone show the same gap for individuals and organisations alike, almost untouched by what is held.

evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
Quoted from section 1.1 Filing alone, and what comes of it, by origin, applicant type and representation of the Stage 2 notebook (open it on GitHub). Everything above says the same in plain English. The code that builds every lens is in analysis/eda/build.py.

**B6 (observational). Standard patents filed alone are rarely granted; the gap is about 36 points for Australian individuals in both decades, and holds among applications that were examined.**
- **Australian individuals:** 4.8% of standard patents filed alone were granted (interval 3.9% to 6.0%) against 40.6% with an attorney (39.2% to 42.1%), FY2010 to FY2019: a gap of 35.8 points (33.9 to 37.5). FY2000 to FY2009: 8.3% against 45.1%, a gap of 36.8 points (34.9 to 38.7).
- **Among those whose examination was requested,** the gap stays: 34.4 points (30.0 to 38.3) and 33.7 (29.5 to 37.6). Filing alone also goes with not asking for examination: 25.2% of individuals' lone applications against 75.9% with an attorney (FY2010 to FY2019).

evidence.title: B5: Australian individuals file alone far more than anyone else; organisations and overseas filers almost never do, for patents
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Split rights by origin (Australian or overseas) and applicant type (individual or organisation).
2. For each group, find the share filed with no attorney or agent, in each decade.
3. Check whether the pattern holds in both decades.

**Which gives observation B5:** Of standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, Australian individuals filed 26.11% with no attorney or agent, Australian organisations 3.54%, overseas individuals 1.14% and overseas organisations 0.28%. For trade marks, Australian individuals filed 68.28% alone.

evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of the standard patents Australian individuals filed alone in FY2010 to FY2019, 4.8% were granted, against 40.6% of those filed with an attorney: a gap of 35.8 points (interval 33.9 to 37.5). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.8 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.4 points).

- **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.2% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.
- **Australian organisations do not show it in both decades:** a gap of 40.0 points in FY2010 to FY2019 but -6.0 in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,149 applications organisations filed alone were granted 62.1% of the time. Those earlier lone filers may have been firms with their own patent staff; the data do not say.
- **Trade marks show it in both decades, for both:** with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more often, organisations' 23.6 points.

evidence.title: M2: Trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it, once other factors are held
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
With no agent recorded before the first renewal, 31.7% of Australians' trade marks filed FY2010 to FY2015 were in force after 10 years, against 50.8% with an attorney. With the filer's type, class, state, route and cohort held together the gap is 14.4 points, 75.5% of the raw 19.1; within individuals and within organisations it holds more fully. Designs show the same at their five-year renewal, almost untouched by what is held.

- **Within each type of filer** the gap holds more fully (85.3% to 94.6% left): individuals -11.8 and -12.0 points, organisations -15.1 and -10.8. Part of the pooled gap is who files alone: individuals, whose marks are less often in force either way (22.3% and 35.6% in FY2010 to FY2015).
- **Designs after 5 years**, FY2010 to FY2019: 30.0% against 46.7%, -16.7 raw and -16.3 held together in the first half; 32.4% against 46.8%, -14.5 and -14.1 in the second.
- B10's raw figures are reproduced (31.7% against 50.8%).

evidence.title: B10: Overseas organisations' trade marks and designs most often stay in force past the first renewal, Australian individuals' least
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **Designs in force after 5 years** (FY2010 to FY2019; FY2005 to FY2009): overseas organisations 69.9% (62.1%), Australian organisations 44.4% (46.4%), Australian individuals 28.2% (27.0%); Australians with an attorney 47.2% (50.8%), alone 28.9% (28.8%). Before the renewal: an attorney 46.7% (50.7%), no agent 31.1% (29.3%); few designs' agents first appear after the renewal fell due (208 at risk, 88.1%).
- Intervals are within about a point for the large groups, and wider for small ones (overseas individuals' designs 33.8% to 40.0% in FY2005 to FY2009). The differences hold in both periods. **Third factors:** applicant type (individuals file alone most, B5), the survival of the business behind a mark, which these data do not hold, and the reverse path above, removed only as far as an agent's arrival is dated.

**B10 (observational). Trade marks and designs: overseas organisations' are most often in force after the first renewal, Australian individuals' least; Australians with no agent before the renewal less often than those with an attorney, by less than representation "at any time" suggested.**
- **Trade marks in force after 10 years** (earliest filing FY2010 to FY2015; FY2003 to FY2009): overseas organisations 56.2% (56.3%), Australian organisations 45.9% (44.6%), overseas individuals 37.9% (40.5%), Australian individuals 26.0% (27.7%). Among Australian filers, by an agent on the record at any time: an attorney 52.0% (52.1%), another agent 34.6% (30.3%), alone 28.6% (30.2%).

evidence.title: B4: The substantive leads, each held in both decades and followed up below
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Beyond the mechanics, the screen points to pairs that bear on the questions: patents filed without an attorney are more often withdrawn; how many countries a patent family reaches varies with the route, the applicant's country and the technology; women's share among inventors varies with the technology; and attorney markets are local.

- **Representation and outcome:** standard patents (0.243; 0.217), trade marks (0.317; 0.274), second-tier patents (0.491; 0.474); designs filed through an agent who is not an attorney (0.323; 0.281). Followed up in B5 to B7.
- **Origin and reach:** the offices a standard patent's family is filed in vary with its route (0.431; 0.481), the applicant's country (0.386; 0.489) and the technology (0.328; 0.31: organic fine chemistry a median of 11). Followed up in B11 and B12.
- **Technology and inventors' gender:** women's estimated share varies with the technology (0.268; 0.297), highest in biotechnology. The apparent links with China are a quirk of the name dictionary (U97), not a finding. Followed up in B17 and B18.

section: How this moves the research forward
evidence.text:
Stage 1 answers none of the five questions. This is how the observation prepares the ground for them.

- **Q2. Who benefits, and who is underserved?** Filing without professional help is a possible sign of a barrier, or of a choice; individuals stand out.
- **Q4. Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?** If filing alone goes with worse outcomes (B6), help for those who file alone is one option IP Australia could weigh; whether it would change outcomes is not tested here.

_Linking an observation to a question is the analyst's guide to where it may help. It is not a finding._

evidence.title: B4: The substantive leads, each held in both decades and followed up below
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: How this moves the research forward
evidence.text:
Stage 2 answers none of the five questions either: it finds which measures go together. This is how the association prepares the ground for them.

- **Q1. What public value does the IP system create?** Lifetimes, reach and citations, the value signals, are tied to who files and in what field, so they must be compared within those groups.
- **Q2. Who benefits, and who is underserved?** Representation and origin go with outcomes, a first sign of who is served well and who is not.
- **Q4. Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?** Filing without an attorney goes with withdrawal, which is where help to file could matter.

_Linking an observation to a question is the analyst's guide to where it may help. It is not a finding._

evidence.title: U2: Five problems in the register were repaired before anything was measured
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (5 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Look for dates that cannot be true (before the register began, or a computer's default date).
2. Compare trade marks' registration dates with their filing dates before 1986.
3. Compare the "technology area" with the class for every type of right.
4. For each right, check whether its agent is one of its own applicants, by identity number or by name.
5. Recount attorney use without those self-agents.

**Which gives observation U2:** Profiling found five quirks: a false end date (1 January 1970) on 1,282 rights; one trade mark registered before the register began; 121,207 old trade marks "registered" on the day they were filed; a "technology area" that only repeated the class for trade marks and designs; and an attorney flag that counted applicants as their own attorneys. Each was repaired.

**U21 (descriptive). Patent attorneys are concentrated; trade mark representation is not.** FY2017 to FY2026, rights filed through an attorney:

events.answer:
**Filing without an attorney is linked with poorer outcomes, especially for Australian individuals’ patents—and most of that gap remains when the analysis holds other recorded factors together. But it does not show that using an attorney causes a better outcome.** That is the central finding of Stage 3’s M1 and M2, both observational findings. [1]

### Who files without an attorney?
Stage 2’s **B5 (observational)** found that Australian individuals were much more likely to file standard patents without an attorney or agent: **26.11%** of their filings in **FY2010 to FY2019**, compared with **3.54%** for Australian organisations, **1.14%** for overseas individuals and **0.28%** for overseas organisations. [2]

### Patents: a large grant gap that survives further testing
Stage 2’s **B6 (observational)** found that, for Australian individuals’ standard patents filed in **FY2010 to FY2019**:
- **4.8%** of those filed alone were granted, compared with **40.6%** filed with an attorney—a gap of **35.8 points**. [3]
- Only **25.2%** of applications filed alone had examination requested, compared with **75.9%** filed with an attorney. [4]

The grant gap was not just about whether applicants requested examination: B6 still found a gap of **34.4 points** among applications whose examination was requested. [5]

Stage 3’s **M1 (observational)** then held the filing route, filing year, state and co-filers together. For **FY2010 to FY2019**, the gap remained **31.2 points**, compared with **35.8 points** before those factors were held together; **87.2%** of the original gap remained. [6] In everyday terms, comparing applications on those recorded characteristics did little to explain away the difference.

M1 classified the link as **“holds”** for individuals in both decades. It was not universal across applicant groups: for Australian organisations in **FY2000 to FY2009**, M1 did not detect a difference either way. [7]

### Trade marks and designs: a similar link with staying in force
Stage 3’s **M2 (observational)** found that **31.7%** of Australians’ trade marks filed in **FY2010 to FY2015** with no agent recorded before the first renewal were still in force after **10 years**, compared with **50.8%** with an attorney. [8] Holding the filer’s type, class, state, route and cohort together reduced the gap from **19.1 points** to **14.4 points**, but most remained. [9]

M2 also found that designs with no agent before their first renewal were less often in force afterwards, with most of the gap remaining when the recorded factors were held together. [10]

### What can—and can’t—we conclude?
**The association is persistent, but it is not evidence of an attorney’s causal effect.** M1 cannot account for the filer’s resources, experience or the merit of the invention, and an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney—so the relationship can also run backwards. [11]

Taken together, M1 and M2 suggest that representation is an important marker of different outcomes, not proof that providing an attorney would close those gaps. [12] The atlas also leaves open whether filing alone reflects a barrier to professional help or a deliberate choice. [13]
